content.title: Why jet lag recovery isn't instant
content.body: Your circadian rhythm—your internal 24-hour clock—runs on light exposure. When you flew from Singapore to London (8-hour timezone shift), your body thought it was 2am when it was actually 10am. Getting less than 7 hours of sleep during this adjustment period increases your anxiety risk by 2.5 times because your brain can't consolidate memories or regulate emotions properly. For an 8-hour shift, your body needs 4 to 8 days to fully sync. You're on Day 3 post-return, so recovery is underway but not complete yet.

metadata.rationale: Build understanding with jet lag science (normalize timeline). DYK Row 3 primers sleep importance. Implementation intention (when-then): educate on mechanism → acceptance of gradual recovery. Position 2 prevents unrealistic expectations.

content.title: Why this jet lag feels harder than usual
content.body: Jet lag alone drains energy, but you're also dealing with anemia (hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, below the 12.0 reference). Low iron means your blood carries less oxygen, so fatigue hits harder. When you add sleep disruption from an 8-hour timezone shift, these two factors compound each other. This double challenge explains why your energy feels particularly low right now. The good news: resetting your circadian rhythm helps even with anemia, and both are addressable.

content.title: One move to reset your body clock faster
content.body: Get sunlight within 30 minutes of waking. Morning light exposure is the most powerful signal to reset your circadian rhythm to Singapore time. It tells your brain 'This is the start of the day,' which helps shift your internal clock. For an 8-hour timezone shift, this typically works within 2 to 3 days. Just 10 to 15 minutes outside—even on your balcony or during a short walk—does the job.

metadata.rationale: Implementation intention (when-then): upon waking → get sunlight. Single micro-action for time-poor achiever. Concrete benefit: 2-3 day timeline. Behavioral activation for circadian reset. Position 4 delivers first actionable payoff.

content.body: Travel disrupted your sleep significantly, but you're already on the road to recovery. This pattern validates that the disruption was external, not a loss of progress.

content.title: Shift your bedtime 30 minutes earlier tonight
content.body: Your bedtime has drifted to 2am post-travel (from 11:30pm before London). Instead of forcing an immediate 11pm bedtime, which can backfire, try moving it 30 minutes earlier tonight to 1:30am. Gradual shifts prevent rebound insomnia and let your body adjust. Then shift another 30 minutes earlier every 2 days. Set an alarm for 1am tonight as a reminder to start winding down.

metadata.rationale: Implementation intention (when-then): 1am alarm → start wind-down. Gentle bedtime shift (not overwhelming). Loss aversion framing: prevent rebound insomnia. Position 6 offers second actionable step for circadian reset.
